tracks.title: Penetration Tester
tracks.description: Learn authorized security assessment, safe lab testing, vulnerability interpretation, and responsible reporting.

levels.label: Level 1 — Beginner
levels.description: Build computer, networking, operating-system, and ethical testing foundations.

levels.label: Level 2 — Intermediate
levels.description: Study web security, assessment methods, and controlled technical analysis.

levels.label: Level 3 — Advanced and Career Preparation
levels.description: Practice scoped case studies, labs, remediation, reporting, and interview readiness.

modules.title: Introduction to Penetration Testing
modules.description: Understand the purpose, authorization, scope, boundaries, and responsible outcomes of a security test.

topics.title: What penetration testing is
objectives: Explain the goal of an authorized assessment.
Distinguish a controlled test from an unauthorized attempt.
topics.definition: Penetration testing is an authorized, scoped assessment that checks whether selected security weaknesses could affect a system.
topics.explanation: A test is planned with an owner, written permission, defined targets, allowed methods, and stop conditions. The tester gathers evidence, validates agreed risks without unnecessary harm, and explains how the owner can reduce them. It is not a guarantee that every weakness was found.
topics.importance: Clear permission and scope protect system owners, users, and testers while keeping findings useful.
steps: Agree on purpose, systems, time window, and contacts.
Review the permitted test plan and safety limits.
Perform only authorized checks in the agreed environment.
Document evidence and recommend fixes for the owner to verify.
topics.example: A building inspector checks only the rooms listed in a signed work order and reports repairs without entering other spaces.
topics.cyberExample: A company authorizes a test of a local training copy of its sign-in page and asks for a report on defensive improvements.

terms.meaning: Explicit permission from the responsible owner for defined activities.
The systems, accounts, data, dates, and methods included in permission.

topics.diagram: WRITTEN PERMISSION -> DEFINED SCOPE -> CONTROLLED REVIEW -> EVIDENCE -> REMEDIATION
topics.demonstration: Example scope statement: 'Review the fictional training portal at local address 127.0.0.1 during the scheduled exercise; no external hosts or real accounts.'
exercise: Read the scope statement above.
Underline what is included and what is excluded.
Write one question to ask before starting if the owner or target is unclear.
topics.expected: The local training portal is the only included target; external hosts and real accounts are excluded.
topics.activity: Practice identifying scope boundaries using the fictional statement; do not contact any other system.
topics.mistakes: A system being publicly reachable is not permission. Verbal assumptions and vague target lists are not safe substitutes for written scope.
keyPoints: Permission must come from the responsible owner.
A test can only support conclusions about the scope and evidence reviewed.
topics.summary: Penetration testing is a controlled, authorized assessment whose value depends on clear scope and responsible reporting.

topics.title: Authorization, scope, and rules of engagement
objectives: Identify the minimum parts of a safe test agreement.
Explain why stop conditions and contacts matter.
topics.definition: Rules of engagement are written instructions describing what a test may do, when it may run, and how people coordinate.
topics.explanation: A safe agreement names the approving owner, target list, excluded systems, time window, data handling rules, emergency contacts, and actions that are not allowed. The tester pauses when a boundary is unclear or an unexpected impact occurs, then asks the owner for direction.
topics.importance: Defined rules reduce outages, privacy exposure, legal confusion, and accidental work outside the approved purpose.
steps: Confirm the authorizing person and target owner.
Compare each target with the written in-scope list.
Review timing, allowed checks, excluded actions, and stop rules.
Record questions and obtain approval before proceeding.
topics.example: A contractor's work order lists one office floor, business hours, and an emergency contact; other floors are excluded.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional lab agreement allows review of a local demo application but forbids testing the public company website.

terms.meaning: Documented limits and coordination instructions for an assessment.
A stated event that requires testing to pause.

topics.diagram: OWNER + TARGETS + TIME + ALLOWED WORK + EXCLUSIONS + CONTACTS
topics.demonstration: If a lab URL redirects to an unfamiliar external domain, stop and confirm whether it is in scope instead of following the redirect.
exercise: Review the fictional agreement in this topic.
List two exclusions and one emergency contact requirement.
Draft a neutral clarification request for an ambiguous target.
topics.expected: A complete agreement identifies the approving owner, exact target, schedule, exclusions, and a way to pause or report impact.
topics.activity: Create a one-paragraph rules-of-engagement checklist for a fictional local practice application.
topics.mistakes: Do not infer that related domains, cloud accounts, or vendor systems are included just because they support the target.
keyPoints: Scope is a boundary, not a suggestion.
Stop and obtain clarification when permission or safety is uncertain.
topics.summary: Written rules define the approved work, safety limits, contacts, and conditions for pausing.

topics.title: A safe assessment lifecycle
objectives: Describe the main stages of an assessment.
Connect evidence to a remediation recommendation.
topics.definition: An assessment lifecycle is an organized sequence for planning, checking, validating, reporting, and reviewing security findings.
topics.explanation: A typical engagement starts with authorization and scope, then reviews the system safely, validates agreed observations, assesses impact, and prepares a report. The owner chooses and implements changes; the tester may later verify fixes if that work is also authorized.
topics.importance: A repeatable lifecycle keeps work focused and makes findings understandable to system owners.
steps: Plan the engagement and confirm authorization.
Review the agreed system and collect relevant evidence.
Validate observations within safety limits.
Report risk, remediation, and any test limitations.
topics.example: A quality inspector plans a checklist, observes a process, records evidence, and explains corrective actions.
topics.cyberExample: A tester reports that a local demo page exposes an unnecessary detail and recommends a specific defensive configuration change.

terms.meaning: Checking whether an observation is accurate and relevant.
A change intended to reduce or remove a security weakness.

topics.diagram: PLAN -> REVIEW -> VALIDATE -> REPORT -> OWNER REMEDIATES -> VERIFY
topics.demonstration: Finding note: 'Observed: the demo page reveals a framework version. Impact: this can aid inventory. Recommendation: limit unnecessary version details and maintain updates.'
exercise: Put the lifecycle stages in order.
For the sample finding, separate the observation from its impact.
Suggest one way the owner could verify the change.
topics.expected: A clear report states what was observed, why it matters, what evidence supports it, and how a defensive fix can be checked.
topics.activity: Write a three-line finding for a fictional training application; do not test a real site.
topics.mistakes: A finding without evidence or a realistic impact can mislead; a test result does not prove that no other weakness exists.
keyPoints: Assessments have limits and should disclose them.
The system owner controls remediation and change approval.
topics.summary: A safe lifecycle connects authorized review to evidence, useful reporting, and owner-led remediation.

topics.title: Assessment types and knowledge levels
objectives: Recognize common assessment perspectives.
Choose an approach that matches a stated learning goal.
topics.definition: Assessment types describe the perspective, knowledge, and scope available to an authorized reviewer.
topics.explanation: A black-box exercise starts with limited design information; a white-box review provides substantial documentation or source context; a gray-box review shares some information. These labels describe setup, not permission. Any approach still needs explicit scope and safe limits.
topics.importance: The chosen perspective affects coverage, time, and what conclusions the report can support.
steps: Define the question the owner wants answered.
Decide what documentation or accounts are provided.
Set the permitted environment and safety boundaries.
Explain how the chosen perspective limits the result.
topics.example: A mystery shopper has little internal information, while a safety auditor receives the building plans before inspection.
topics.cyberExample: A local coding exercise may provide source code for a defensive review, while a separate approved lab may provide only a user-facing demo.

terms.meaning: An assessment perspective with limited internal design information.
A review perspective with substantial internal documentation or code context.
A perspective with some, but not all, internal context.

topics.diagram: LIMITED CONTEXT: BLACK BOX | SOME CONTEXT: GRAY BOX | BROAD CONTEXT: WHITE BOX
topics.demonstration: All three approaches require a named owner, an approved target, and clear exclusions.
exercise: Choose a perspective for reviewing a fictional source-code sample.
Choose a perspective for a usability-focused review of a local demo.
Explain one limitation of each choice.
topics.expected: Source review is suited to broad internal context; a user-view exercise can use limited context, while both remain strictly authorized.
topics.activity: Compare the fictional scenarios and state which information the reviewer would receive.
topics.mistakes: Calling an exercise black-box does not make it safe or authorized, and no assessment type guarantees complete coverage.
keyPoints: Knowledge level changes the review perspective.
Authorization and safety rules apply to every assessment type.
topics.summary: Choose an assessment perspective based on the owner's question and document its limits.

quiz.prompt: What makes a penetration test authorized?
choices: Explicit permission and a defined scope from the responsible owner
quiz.explanation: A test requires permission from the owner and clear boundaries for targets and methods.

quiz.prompt: What should you do when a target is not clearly listed in the scope?
quiz.explanation: Unclear targets are outside safe assumptions; obtain approval before continuing.

quiz.prompt: Who decides and implements remediation?
choices: The system owner through approved change processes
quiz.explanation: The system owner is responsible for approving and implementing changes.

quiz.prompt: Does a black-box assessment remove the need for written permission?
quiz.explanation: All assessment types require authorization and defined scope.

quiz.prompt: What can an assessment conclude?
choices: What the available evidence supports within its scope and limits
That every weakness in the organization was found
That every related vendor system was tested
quiz.explanation: A report should state the scope and limitations rather than claim complete coverage.

modules.title: Networking Fundamentals for Penetration Testers
modules.description: Build an accurate mental model of how data moves between systems, how network boundaries work, and why authorization applies to every assessment.

learningIntroduction.meaning: Computer networking is the set of agreed rules and devices that let systems exchange information.
learningIntroduction.whyLearn: Network concepts help a tester interpret architecture, ask useful scope questions, and explain defensive findings without guessing from a tool output.
learningIntroduction.jobUse: Penetration testers use network diagrams, address plans, service inventories, and written scope to understand an approved environment and communicate its boundaries.
learningIntroduction.outcomes: You will be able to describe packet delivery, address and name resolution, common transport behavior, segmentation, and safe documentation practices.

learningObjectives: Describe how encapsulation and network layers organize communication.
Distinguish IP addresses, names, ports, and application protocols.
Explain the basic roles of TCP, UDP, DNS, routers, and network segments.
Read a simple fictional network diagram and identify trust boundaries.
State why written authorization and a defined target list are essential.
modules.moduleSummary: Network assessment starts with an accurate map and explicit permission, not with assumptions. Addresses identify network interfaces, names help people locate services, transport protocols deliver data, and application protocols define its meaning. Segmentation and trust boundaries describe how exposure is limited. The concepts here support safe analysis and clear reporting; they do not authorize testing any real system.
keyConcepts: Encapsulation adds layer-specific information as data moves through a network stack.
An IP address identifies a network interface for routing; it is not proof of ownership or permission.
A port identifies an application endpoint within a host and transport protocol.
DNS maps names to records; it does not establish that a resolved destination is in scope.
TCP provides ordered, acknowledged delivery while UDP has lower-overhead datagrams without those guarantees.
Segmentation and documented trust boundaries limit unnecessary communication.

glossary.meaning: A formatted unit of network-layer data carried between network interfaces.
A link-layer unit used to move data across a local network segment.
The process of adding protocol information as data passes through network layers.
A numeric address used to identify an interface for network-layer delivery.
A defined portion of an IP address space treated as a network segment.
The Domain Name System, which stores records that associate names with network-related information.
A numbered transport-layer endpoint used to direct traffic to an application service.
A transport protocol that provides ordered delivery and retransmission mechanisms.
A datagram transport protocol that does not itself guarantee delivery or ordering.
Separating systems into network zones to control and reduce communication.
A point where access, identity, or security assumptions change.
The written targets, dates, methods, and limits explicitly authorized for an assessment.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you explain the difference between an IP address and a port?
interviewQuestions.answer: An IP address identifies a network interface for routing, while a port identifies an application endpoint associated with a transport protocol. Neither one establishes ownership or permission to test.

interviewQuestions.question: What does DNS do, and what does it not tell a tester?
interviewQuestions.answer: DNS provides records that help map names to network information. A result can inform an approved inventory, but it does not prove that the destination belongs to the client or is in scope.

interviewQuestions.question: When might TCP be selected instead of UDP?
interviewQuestions.answer: An application may use TCP when it needs ordered, acknowledged delivery and retransmission behavior. Protocol choice depends on the application's requirements, not on a claim that one is universally safer.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is segmentation important in a security review?
interviewQuestions.answer: Segmentation limits which systems can communicate and helps contain exposure. I would compare the documented design with approved evidence, then report any verified mismatch to the system owner.

revisionTopics: Sketch how application data is encapsulated into transport, network, and link information.
Review the difference between a hostname, IP address, port, and service protocol.
Compare TCP and UDP guarantees and typical design considerations.
Explain how routers and segments create boundaries in a network diagram.
Practice separating observations from assumptions in a fictional scope document.

topics.title: Packets, frames, and network layers
objectives: Describe the purpose of protocol layers.
Trace a simplified message from an application to a local link.
topics.definition: A network stack divides communication into layers so each part can handle a smaller, well-defined responsibility.
topics.explanation: An application creates meaningful content, a transport protocol organizes delivery between application endpoints, and the network layer helps route data between networks. A local link then carries a frame to the next device. Each layer adds or interprets its own metadata, a process called encapsulation. Real packet formats are more detailed, but the layered model is useful for explaining where a communication problem or control belongs.
topics.importance: Layered thinking helps a reviewer distinguish a routing question from an application behavior and describe evidence precisely.
steps: Start with an application message and identify its intended service.
Identify the transport behavior used by that application.
Place the network-layer source and destination information around the transport data.
Describe the local link that carries the data to the next network device.
topics.example: Mail is written, placed in an addressed envelope, sorted by a delivery service, and carried by a local courier; each step has a different role.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional diagram can show a browser application communicating through a transport endpoint and router to a training server.

terms.meaning: A conceptual group of network responsibilities.
Adding layer-specific protocol information around data.
A link-layer unit delivered on a local network segment.

topics.diagram:
APPLICATION DATA
  ↓ transport information
  ↓ network addressing
  ↓ local-link frame
  → next network device
topics.demonstration: In a paper exercise, label the application message, transport endpoint, network addresses, and local-link frame. No network connection is needed.
exercise: Draw four nested labels for a fictional message.
Write one responsibility beside each layer.
Mark where a local router would receive and forward the traffic.
topics.expected: The drawing separates application meaning, transport delivery, network routing, and local-link delivery.
topics.activity: Use a notebook or offline diagram editor to explain the trip from a fictional laptop to a lab server.
topics.mistakes: A layer model is a teaching abstraction, not a guarantee that every implementation has identical internal behavior. Do not treat an observed address as proof of ownership.
keyPoints: Each layer addresses a different responsibility.
Encapsulation adds metadata that supports delivery.
A router makes forwarding decisions at network boundaries.
topics.summary: Layered models make network behavior easier to explain and troubleshoot without confusing application data with delivery metadata.

topics.title: IP addresses and private network ranges
objectives: Explain the role of an IP address.
Recognize that address ranges alone do not define assessment permission.
topics.definition: An IP address is a network-layer identifier used to deliver data to an interface.
topics.explanation: IPv4 uses four decimal octets and IPv6 uses a larger hexadecimal address format. Networks divide address space into prefixes, often written with a prefix length. Private ranges are intended for internal use and documentation ranges are reserved for examples, but an address's format does not identify its owner, contents, or authorization status. Real engagement scope must come from the owner-approved target list.
topics.importance: Addressing is essential for reading inventories and diagrams, while confusing location with permission can cause unsafe testing.
steps: Read the complete address and its address family.
Identify the documented prefix or network segment.
Compare the address to the owner-approved scope and exclusions.
Record uncertainty and ask the responsible contact before any action.
topics.example: A street number helps route a delivery but does not tell a visitor whether they have permission to enter the building.
topics.cyberExample: A sample diagram may use 192.0.2.0/24 for a fictional documentation network and 127.0.0.1 for a local-only example.

terms.meaning: An Internet Protocol version using 32-bit addresses.
An Internet Protocol version using 128-bit addresses.
A notation indicating how many leading address bits identify a network.

topics.diagram:
FICTIONAL DIAGRAM: 192.0.2.0/24
Host A: 192.0.2.10
Host B: 192.0.2.20
Documentation only — not a target list
topics.demonstration: Compare the sample addresses 192.0.2.10 and 192.0.2.20 with the fictional prefix 192.0.2.0/24 and note that both are in the example segment.
exercise: Label 192.0.2.0/24 as fictional documentation data.
Identify the two sample hosts shown in the diagram.
Write a reminder that the diagram is not authorization.
topics.expected: The learner can interpret the example segment while clearly stating that it authorizes no network activity.
topics.activity: Annotate an offline address plan with owner, environment, segment, and explicit in-scope/out-of-scope labels.
topics.mistakes: Private or familiar-looking addresses do not imply that a system is safe to contact. A subnet match does not expand the written scope.
keyPoints: Addresses support routing, not identity verification.
Prefix notation describes a network range.
Only the approved scope authorizes assessment work.
topics.summary: IP addressing helps organize an inventory, but only documented owner permission determines what may be assessed.

topics.title: Routers, switches, and local delivery
objectives: Distinguish basic router and switch responsibilities.
Identify where network boundaries appear on a diagram.
topics.definition: Switches connect devices within a local network, while routers forward traffic between IP networks.
topics.explanation: A switch commonly moves local frames based on link-layer information. A router examines network-layer destinations and selects a next hop according to its routing information. Real environments may combine these functions in one device and add firewalls or other controls. A diagram should show logical segments and boundaries rather than imply that every network is a single flat space.
topics.importance: Understanding device roles helps explain how traffic is segmented and where defensive controls may apply.
steps: Identify the local segment containing a device.
Trace local delivery through a switch when appropriate.
Mark the router or gateway between distinct IP networks.
Record any firewall or policy boundary shown in the design.
topics.example: A building's internal mailroom sorts local deliveries while a central depot sends mail between cities.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional test diagram can show a learner workstation and a lab server on separate segments with a documented gateway between them.

terms.meaning: A device that forwards frames within a local network.
A device that forwards packets between IP networks.
A network point used to reach destinations beyond a local segment.

topics.diagram: WORKSTATION -- switch -- local segment -- router/firewall -- lab segment -- server
topics.demonstration: On paper, trace a fictional packet to a host on another segment and mark the router as the transition point.
exercise: Draw two segments and place one host in each.
Add a switch to each local segment and a router between them.
Mark where a policy could limit communication.
topics.expected: The diagram shows that local switching and inter-network routing are different responsibilities.
topics.activity: Review a supplied fictional architecture and circle each routing and trust boundary.
topics.mistakes: A device label does not prove that a security policy is active. Validate design claims only through approved documentation and evidence.
keyPoints: Switching usually supports local delivery.
Routing connects distinct IP networks.
Firewalls and access controls can enforce boundaries.
topics.summary: Network devices provide local and inter-network delivery, while documented controls define how segments may communicate.

topics.title: Subnets and network diagrams
objectives: Interpret a basic subnet notation.
Explain how a diagram can record scope and trust boundaries.
topics.definition: A subnet is a defined block of IP addresses treated as one network segment.
topics.explanation: Prefix notation describes the portion of an address reserved for the network, while the remaining bits identify addresses within it. A subnet plan helps teams organize services and route traffic. For a security assessment, a diagram should include labels such as environment, owner, and scope status, because an address range alone omits operational context.
topics.importance: Subnets help teams reason about reachability and segmentation, but a clear diagram must also communicate ownership and test limits.
steps: Read the network prefix shown in the plan.
List the example systems attached to the segment.
Mark connections to other segments and controls.
Add explicit in-scope and excluded labels from the approved agreement.
topics.example: A campus map shows buildings and gates; the map helps plan routes but does not grant access to restricted rooms.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional diagram labels one training subnet as in scope and a vendor network as excluded.

terms.meaning: An IP address block configured as a network segment.
A notation for representing an IP network and its prefix length.
A visual record of systems, connections, segments, and boundaries.

topics.diagram:
TRAINING SEGMENT: 192.0.2.0/24 [IN SCOPE BY AGREEMENT]
VENDOR SEGMENT: separate boundary [EXCLUDED]
topics.demonstration: The documentation-only prefix 192.0.2.0/24 is an example label; it should never be used as evidence that any actual target is approved.
exercise: Sketch a two-segment fictional network.
Label the approved training segment and excluded vendor segment.
Add the owner and the written agreement reference to the sketch.
topics.expected: The drawing communicates both connectivity and the explicit scope boundary.
topics.activity: Prepare a one-page offline diagram for a fictional lab, showing systems, segments, owners, and exclusions.
topics.mistakes: Do not infer that every host in a range belongs to the same owner or is covered by one authorization.
keyPoints: Subnet prefixes describe address organization.
Diagrams should show logical boundaries.
Scope comes from the approved agreement, not the diagram alone.
topics.summary: A well-labeled subnet diagram supports safer planning by separating network organization from authorization.

topics.title: TCP and UDP fundamentals
objectives: Compare TCP and UDP delivery behavior.
Relate transport selection to application needs.
topics.definition: TCP and UDP are transport protocols that deliver application data with different reliability and overhead characteristics.
topics.explanation: TCP establishes a connection and uses sequence information, acknowledgements, and retransmission to support ordered delivery. UDP sends independent datagrams without providing those same delivery guarantees. Applications can add their own reliability or accept occasional loss depending on their needs. Neither protocol is inherently secure; confidentiality and integrity require appropriate protections at other layers.
topics.importance: Knowing the difference helps interpret an architecture and avoid claiming that a transport choice alone makes a service safe.
steps: Identify the application requirement for ordering or loss tolerance.
Check which transport behavior supports that requirement.
Identify any higher-layer security controls separately.
Document the protocol from approved design information.
topics.example: A signed-for parcel service confirms delivery, while a quick announcement may be sent without waiting for acknowledgements.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional service inventory may document a reliable administrative application over TCP and a time-sensitive media flow using UDP.

terms.meaning: Connection-oriented transport that supports ordered, acknowledged delivery.
Datagram transport without built-in ordered-delivery guarantees.
A protocol that supports communication between application endpoints.

topics.diagram:
TCP: data → acknowledgement → possible retransmission
UDP: datagram → best-effort delivery
topics.demonstration: Annotate the two paths with delivery guarantees; do not generate or send packets.
exercise: Choose which path offers acknowledgements.
Name one application need that might favor low-overhead datagrams.
Explain why neither choice guarantees encryption.
topics.expected: The learner distinguishes transport reliability from confidentiality and application security.
topics.activity: Classify fictional application descriptions by delivery requirement using a paper table.
topics.mistakes: UDP is not always faster in practice, and TCP does not automatically encrypt data. Security depends on the full design.
keyPoints: TCP supports ordered, acknowledged delivery.
UDP sends datagrams without those built-in guarantees.
Encryption is a separate security property.
topics.summary: Transport protocols offer different delivery behavior, while application requirements and separate security layers determine the complete design.

topics.title: Ports and application services
objectives: Explain what a port represents.
Interpret a service inventory without treating it as permission.
topics.definition: A port is a numbered endpoint used with a transport protocol to direct data to an application service.
topics.explanation: A host may offer several applications, and port numbers help distinguish their transport endpoints. A service inventory records expected protocols, owners, and business purpose. Well-known port conventions are useful hints, not proof of what is running. An assessment should use only information and checks allowed by the written scope.
topics.importance: Service inventories help owners reduce unnecessary exposure and help reviewers describe system architecture accurately.
steps: Read the host and transport protocol in the approved inventory.
Note the listed endpoint and service owner.
Compare expected exposure with the documented business need.
Report discrepancies using evidence gathered by permitted means.
topics.example: An office extension identifies a desk phone, but the extension number alone does not identify who is present.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional asset register lists a training web service with an owner, purpose, and approved maintenance window.

terms.meaning: A numeric transport endpoint associated with an application.
A maintained list of services, owners, purpose, and expected exposure.
A conventionally assigned port number commonly associated with a protocol.

topics.diagram:
HOST ADDRESS + TRANSPORT + PORT → APPLICATION ENDPOINT
Inventory evidence ≠ authorization
topics.demonstration: Review a made-up table with columns for host, protocol, port, owner, and approved scope; identify missing ownership information.
exercise: Label each field in the sample inventory.
Highlight an endpoint with no listed owner.
Write a safe clarification question for the asset owner.
topics.expected: The inventory review identifies missing context without contacting or probing a system.
topics.activity: Build an offline service inventory for fictional lab components and include an owner and purpose for each.
topics.mistakes: A familiar port number does not prove which application is running. A listed endpoint is not automatically an approved target.
keyPoints: Ports distinguish application endpoints.
Inventories should include owner and business purpose.
Conventions are clues, not verified evidence.
topics.summary: Port knowledge helps interpret inventories, but ownership, evidence, and scope must be established separately.

topics.title: DNS and name resolution
objectives: Describe the purpose of DNS.
Explain why a resolved name does not establish scope.
topics.definition: DNS is a distributed naming system that provides records used to associate domain names with network information.
topics.explanation: People use memorable names while networks use address and service records to support communication. Resolvers may cache results, and records can change as infrastructure evolves. A domain can point to shared or third-party services, so name resolution is only one part of understanding an architecture. Authorization and ownership must be confirmed independently.
topics.importance: Name resolution affects service discovery and reliability, while shared hosting and changing records make ownership checks important.
steps: Read the name and record type in approved documentation.
Check the record's owner and intended environment.
Note that cached or changing results may differ over time.
Confirm that any related infrastructure is explicitly in scope.
topics.example: A phone directory links a person's name to a number, but the entry alone does not show who currently answers.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional architecture lists a training name and its owner-approved address in an offline workbook.

terms.meaning: A service that looks up DNS records on behalf of a client.
A stored DNS data entry such as an address or mail-routing record.
A temporary copy of data kept to answer repeated requests efficiently.

topics.diagram:
APPLICATION NAME → DNS LOOKUP → RECORD / ADDRESS
Owner + scope must be verified separately
topics.demonstration: Given fictional records for `training.example` and `mail.example`, identify their listed purpose without performing live lookups.
exercise: Read a supplied fictional DNS table.
Mark which entries describe web, mail, or alias information.
List two facts the table does not prove about ownership or permission.
topics.expected: The learner identifies record purpose and states that DNS data alone cannot authorize testing.
topics.activity: Create a fictional name-resolution table for a classroom diagram, then label it documentation-only.
topics.mistakes: A subdomain or redirect is not automatically included in a test. DNS data may be stale or may represent shared infrastructure.
keyPoints: DNS maps names to records used by applications.
Records can change or be cached.
Every destination still needs owner and scope confirmation.
topics.summary: DNS supports naming and service delivery, but its results must be interpreted with current ownership and scope information.

topics.title: Segmentation, firewalls, and trust boundaries
objectives: Explain why networks are segmented.
Identify trust boundaries and policy assumptions in a fictional design.
topics.definition: Network segmentation divides systems into zones and uses policies to limit communication between them.
topics.explanation: Organizations separate systems according to purpose, sensitivity, or operational need. Firewalls and access-control rules can define allowed flows between zones, while identity-aware controls add user and device context. A diagram shows intended design, but evidence is needed to confirm how a control behaves. A reviewer should record what was authorized and avoid crossing a boundary without explicit approval.
topics.importance: Well-designed boundaries reduce unnecessary access and can limit the impact of a compromised or misconfigured system.
steps: Identify the zones and the data or services each one supports.
Trace only the flows shown in approved design documents.
Mark policy controls and the owner responsible for them.
Report an observed mismatch through the agreed channel.
topics.example: A hospital separates public waiting areas from staff-only rooms with doors and access rules.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional company diagram separates a learner workstation, application tier, and data tier with documented permitted flows.

terms.meaning: Dividing a network to control communication between groups of systems.
A control that permits or blocks traffic according to policy.
A point where access assumptions or security controls change.

topics.diagram: USER ZONE -- approved flow -- APPLICATION ZONE -- restricted flow -- DATA ZONE
topics.demonstration: On a fictional diagram, mark the data zone as restricted and note that only the owner-approved application flow is expected.
exercise: Draw three fictional zones.
Mark one approved flow and one prohibited flow from supplied policy text.
Write a report sentence that distinguishes intended policy from verified behavior.
topics.expected: The learner identifies boundaries and avoids claiming that a diagram proves control operation.
topics.activity: Compare an offline architecture diagram with fictional firewall rules and list questions for the owner.
topics.mistakes: A network diagram may be outdated, and a firewall label does not prove a rule is correct or effective.
keyPoints: Segmentation limits communication based on policy.
Trust boundaries are important scope and design checkpoints.
Validate claims only with authorized evidence.
topics.summary: Segmentation creates useful boundaries when policies match the intended design and are maintained by the system owner.

quiz.prompt: What does encapsulation describe?
choices: Adding protocol information as data passes through layers
Deleting a packet at every router
Changing a hostname into a user account
Turning a diagram into an authorization
quiz.explanation: Each layer adds or interprets metadata needed for its communication responsibility.
quiz.distractorNote: Layering does not mean data is deleted or transformed into an identity record.

quiz.prompt: What does an IP address primarily help a network do?
choices: Grant permission to test a host
quiz.explanation: IP addresses support network-layer delivery; ownership and authorization require separate evidence.
quiz.distractorNote: An address is not an ownership or authorization credential.

quiz.prompt: Which device role most directly forwards traffic between IP networks?
quiz.explanation: Routers forward packets between networks using routing information.
quiz.distractorNote: End-user peripherals and applications do not perform this network forwarding role.

quiz.prompt: What does a subnet prefix describe?
choices: The network portion of an address range
quiz.explanation: A prefix length identifies how much of the address belongs to the network portion.
quiz.distractorNote: Address notation provides no permission decision.

quiz.prompt: Which transport offers built-in acknowledgements and ordered delivery?
quiz.explanation: TCP uses mechanisms such as acknowledgements and sequencing to support ordered delivery.
quiz.distractorNote: UDP is datagram-based, and DNS is an application-layer naming system.

quiz.prompt: Does TCP by itself guarantee that application data is encrypted?
choices: Only when a hostname is present
quiz.explanation: TCP provides transport delivery behavior; encryption is a separate security control.
quiz.distractorNote: Encryption must be provided by an appropriate security protocol or application design.

quiz.prompt: What does a port number help identify?
choices: An application endpoint associated with a transport protocol
The owner of an IP range
quiz.explanation: Ports distinguish transport endpoints so data can be directed to an application service.
quiz.distractorNote: Port numbers do not encode physical location or scope approval.

quiz.prompt: What can a DNS record tell you?
choices: That a destination is automatically in scope
That a system has no security issues
That all records are current and complete
quiz.explanation: DNS records provide naming and service-related information, but they do not establish authorization or security posture.
quiz.distractorNote: A name resolving successfully does not establish client ownership or permission.

quiz.prompt: What is a common purpose of network segmentation?
choices: Removing the need for access policy
Guaranteeing that no incident can occur
quiz.explanation: Segmentation uses zones and policies to reduce unnecessary connectivity and contain exposure.
quiz.distractorNote: Segmentation reduces risk but does not replace policy or guarantee prevention.

quiz.prompt: A system appears in a fictional subnet diagram. What authorizes testing it?
choices: Explicit owner permission and written scope
Its presence on the diagram alone
quiz.explanation: Only the responsible owner's explicit authorization and defined scope permit assessment work.
quiz.distractorNote: Maps and address ranges describe architecture; they do not grant permission.

modules.title: Linux for Ethical Hackers
modules.description: Learn safe, read-only Linux navigation, files, users, permissions, processes, logs, and maintenance concepts in a local training environment.

learningIntroduction.meaning: Linux is a family of operating systems used on servers, cloud platforms, appliances, and many security tools.
learningIntroduction.whyLearn: A clear understanding of Linux makes it easier to interpret authorized system documentation, communicate with administrators, and recognize when a configuration needs review.
learningIntroduction.jobUse: Penetration testers and defenders encounter Linux systems in controlled labs and client environments; they need to understand accounts, permissions, services, and evidence without making unapproved changes.
learningIntroduction.outcomes: You will navigate a local training VM with read-only commands, explain common directories and access controls, and describe safe evidence-handling practices.

learningObjectives: Distinguish a terminal, shell, command, and Linux distribution.
Navigate the filesystem and describe common directory purposes.
Explain users, groups, ownership, permissions, and least privilege.
Interpret process, service, and log concepts using fictional examples.
Describe safe package maintenance and protect original evidence.
modules.moduleSummary: Linux literacy begins with understanding the environment and observing it carefully. The shell can make routine inspection efficient, but commands should be limited to the approved local environment and read-only tasks unless a system owner explicitly authorizes more. Ownership, least privilege, service management, updates, and trustworthy logs are core operational concepts. Preserve originals, record context, and ask before changing a system.
keyConcepts: A shell interprets commands; a terminal provides an interface for interacting with it.
Filesystem paths describe where files and directories are located.
Users, groups, ownership, and permissions control access to resources.
Processes are running program instances; services are managed background functions.
Logs provide time-stamped records that need context and integrity checks.
Updates should follow a tested, approved maintenance process.

glossary.meaning: A packaged Linux operating system built from a kernel and selected software.
A text-based interface that accepts input and displays command output.
A program that interprets commands and provides an interactive environment.
A sequence of directory names that locates a file or directory.
The privileged administrative account on many Linux systems.
Providing only the access necessary for a defined task.
A running instance of a program.
A background function managed by the operating system.
A record of system or application events, often with timestamps.
A system tool that installs, updates, and tracks software packages.
The user and group associated with a filesystem object.
The property that data remains complete and unchanged unless an authorized change is recorded.

interviewQuestions.question: How do a terminal and a shell differ?
interviewQuestions.answer: A terminal is the interface for text input and output. A shell is the program that interprets commands entered through that interface.

interviewQuestions.question: Why should security work follow least privilege?
interviewQuestions.answer: Least privilege limits accidental changes and reduces the impact of a compromised account. I would use only the access approved for the task and request elevation through the owner's process if required.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a process and a service?
interviewQuestions.answer: A process is a running program instance. A service is a background capability that is often managed by the operating system and may be implemented by one or more processes.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you approach an unfamiliar system log?
interviewQuestions.answer: I would confirm the source, time zone, collection method, and retention context, then interpret entries cautiously. I would preserve the original and avoid treating one log line as conclusive proof.

revisionTopics: Review terminal, shell, command, distribution, and path terminology.
Identify common filesystem areas and distinguish system files from user data.
Practice explaining user, group, ownership, and permission concepts.
Compare a process with a service and describe where logs fit.
Explain why package changes and evidence handling need owner-approved procedures.

topics.title: Distributions, terminal, and shell
objectives: Identify common parts of a Linux command-line environment.
Explain why commands should be reviewed before use.
topics.definition: A Linux command-line environment combines an operating-system distribution, a terminal interface, and a shell that interprets commands.
topics.explanation: A distribution packages the Linux kernel with tools, libraries, and an update process. A terminal displays input and output, while a shell interprets commands and may expand paths or variables. Different systems can use different distributions and shells, so instructions should be checked against the local environment. For beginner practice, use a disposable training VM and observe with read-only commands.
topics.importance: Knowing the environment prevents applying the wrong instructions and helps keep a review within the approved system.
steps: Confirm that the machine is the designated local training VM.
Identify the distribution and shell from provided documentation.
Read each command and understand its expected effect before use.
Prefer read-only inspection until a system owner authorizes a change.
topics.example: A kitchen has a work surface and a person following a recipe; the surface is not the recipe interpreter.
topics.cyberExample: A learner compares the VM's documented distribution with a course guide before using its examples.

terms.meaning: A packaged Linux operating-system environment.
An interface for text input and output.
A command interpreter used by a user or script.

topics.diagram: LEARNER → TERMINAL → SHELL → APPROVED LOCAL OPERATING SYSTEM
topics.demonstration: In a local VM, read the course's environment label and identify which interface accepts input and which program interprets it.
exercise: Record the training VM name from its local course label.
Identify the shell from instructor-provided documentation.
Write down one reason to inspect a command before running it.
topics.expected: The learner can explain the local interface and avoids assuming that an online command applies to every distribution.
topics.activity: Use the course-provided disposable VM only; list environment facts from its welcome screen without connecting to any remote host.
topics.mistakes: A shell is not the operating system itself, and a command copied from an unknown source may change files or system state.
keyPoints: Distribution, terminal, and shell have distinct roles.
Instructions can vary across systems.
Use read-only local observation unless changes are authorized.
topics.summary: First identify the local environment, then understand a command's behavior before using it.

topics.title: Filesystem layout and paths
objectives: Describe the purpose of a path.
Recognize common Linux filesystem areas at a high level.
topics.definition: The Linux filesystem organizes files and directories into a tree that begins at a root directory.
topics.explanation: A path names a location in that tree, either from the root or relative to the current directory. Common areas may hold configuration, user files, logs, programs, or temporary data, though exact layout can vary. Understanding the path helps confirm what a file represents before reading it. Never assume that a path is safe to modify because it appears familiar.
topics.importance: Correct path interpretation reduces mistakes and supports careful evidence collection.
steps: Identify whether a path is absolute or relative.
Read directory names from the root toward the target.
Use documentation to infer the directory's purpose.
Confirm the file and permission context before accessing it.
topics.example: A filing cabinet uses folders and subfolders to locate a document.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional system map separates configuration examples, learner files, and sample logs.

terms.meaning: The top of the filesystem tree, represented by a slash.
A path that starts at the filesystem root.
A path interpreted from the current working directory.

topics.diagram:
/
|-- etc/   configuration
|-- home/  user areas
|-- var/   changing data and logs
+-- usr/   shared programs and resources
topics.demonstration: Read the sample tree above and describe the purpose labels; treat them as common conventions, not universal guarantees.
exercise: Circle the root in the sample tree.
Identify which illustrative area could contain user files.
Explain why checking a path is important before a change.
topics.expected: The learner distinguishes absolute and relative paths and treats directory names as clues to verify.
topics.activity: Annotate an offline filesystem tree with the data each fictional directory may contain.
topics.mistakes: Do not confuse a directory name with proof of its contents, and do not write to system paths without explicit approval.
keyPoints: Paths locate objects in a tree.
Absolute paths begin at root; relative paths depend on context.
Directory purpose can vary by distribution and configuration.
topics.summary: Filesystem literacy means reading path context carefully and verifying a file's role before interacting with it.

topics.title: Safe navigation and reading sample files
objectives: Use simple read-only navigation concepts.
Distinguish observation from a system change.
topics.definition: Read-only navigation gathers information without intentionally modifying files or system configuration.
topics.explanation: Basic commands such as `pwd`, `ls`, and reading a course-provided sample file can help a learner understand the current location and available training data. Output should be interpreted in the context of the VM, user, and time. Avoid destructive or privileged commands, and do not copy instructions to a production system. If a task requires a change, pause and obtain the system owner's approval.
topics.importance: Careful observation builds confidence while reducing the chance of altering evidence or disrupting a system.
steps: Open only the designated local training VM.
Confirm the current directory using a read-only navigation command.
List only the course-provided sample directory.
Read a supplied fictional text file and record its local path.
topics.example: A librarian checks a catalog entry and reads a permitted reference book without rearranging the archive.
topics.cyberExample: The learner reviews a provided sample inventory file stored inside the course VM.

terms.meaning: The directory a shell uses as the current context for relative paths.
An operation that observes data without changing it.
Fictional or prepared material used for instruction.

topics.diagram: CONFIRM LOCAL VM → CHECK LOCATION → LIST COURSE SAMPLE → READ FICTIONAL FILE
topics.demonstration: The safe exercise uses only documented read-only navigation and a course-provided text file; no privileged, network, or modification command is needed.
exercise: Use the VM's course instructions to locate its prepared sample folder.
Read the sample file using the documented read-only viewer.
Record the filename and one observation without editing or copying it elsewhere.
topics.expected: The sample is observed in place and the learner can report its location without changing its contents.
topics.activity: Complete the exercise in a disposable local VM; do not use administrative access or connect to a real system.
topics.mistakes: A command that looks familiar can still modify data. Check flags, paths, and permissions; stop when the effect is unclear.
keyPoints: Use only the designated local environment.
Read-only observation is preferred for introductory practice.
Preserve sample data and pause if any command's effect is uncertain.
topics.summary: Safe navigation is deliberate, local, and read-only, with course-provided examples kept intact.

topics.title: Configuration files and data handling
objectives: Explain why configuration requires careful handling.
Describe a safe approach to fictional configuration review.
topics.definition: Configuration files store settings that influence how an operating system or application behaves.
topics.explanation: Configuration can include service behavior, access rules, and references to sensitive values. A reviewer should use approved copies or read-only views, limit exposure of secrets, and preserve the original source. Findings need enough context for an owner to reproduce the observation without including unnecessary private data. Any proposed change should follow a change-management process.
topics.importance: Configuration mistakes can affect confidentiality, availability, and integrity, while careless copying can expose secrets.
steps: Confirm the file is a fictional sample or explicitly approved source.
Review its purpose and owner before interpreting values.
Avoid copying passwords, tokens, or personal data into notes.
Record a redacted observation and preserve the original.
topics.example: An auditor reviews a redacted settings sheet and records the missing control without copying private account details.
topics.cyberExample: A sample application configuration contains a placeholder value labeled `REDACTED`; the learner notes the policy issue without seeking a real secret.

terms.meaning: Settings that control software or system behavior.
Sensitive authentication or cryptographic data that must be protected.
Removing or masking sensitive information before sharing evidence.

topics.diagram: APPROVED COPY → READ-ONLY REVIEW → REDACTED NOTE → OWNER-APPROVED CHANGE
topics.demonstration: The fictional sample contains placeholder values only. Record the setting name and concern, not a credential.
exercise: Inspect the fictional configuration excerpt in the course workbook.
Mark which values are placeholders and which require owner review.
Write a redacted finding that does not repeat sensitive values.
topics.expected: The note describes the configuration issue without exposing secrets or changing the sample.
topics.activity: Draft a safe, redacted observation from a fictional configuration worksheet.
topics.mistakes: Do not paste secrets into tickets, screenshots, or chat. Do not edit a live configuration during a review without explicit change approval.
keyPoints: Configuration influences system behavior.
Treat credentials and personal information as sensitive.
Preserve originals and report through approved channels.
topics.summary: Configuration review should protect sensitive values, preserve original data, and separate observation from change.

topics.title: Users, groups, and least privilege
objectives: Explain how users and groups support access control.
Apply least-privilege reasoning to a fictional role.
topics.definition: Linux user and group identities help determine who may access files and perform administrative actions.
topics.explanation: A user represents an account, and a group can organize accounts that share a defined need. Ownership and permissions govern access to filesystem objects, while administrative privileges enable more extensive changes. The principle of least privilege limits each identity to the permissions required for its task. A reviewer should not attempt to elevate access or use another person's credentials.
topics.importance: Appropriate access limits reduce accidental damage and constrain the impact of compromised accounts.
steps: Identify the role and its approved task.
List the files and capabilities actually required.
Compare the fictional access with the least-privilege goal.
Recommend an owner-reviewed permission change when evidence supports it.
topics.example: A library card grants access to the resources needed by a member, not the authority to alter the building's records.
topics.cyberExample: A read-only analyst account can review sample logs without having rights to change system settings.

terms.meaning: An account identity associated with processes and access rights.
A set of accounts used to manage shared permissions.
Granting only the access required for a task.

topics.diagram: IDENTITY → GROUP MEMBERSHIP → RESOURCE OWNER + PERMISSIONS → ALLOWED ACTION
topics.demonstration: Classify three fictional roles as read-only reviewer, application operator, and system administrator, then match only necessary sample permissions.
exercise: Read the role descriptions in the workbook.
Mark which sample files each role needs to read.
Identify one permission that should be reviewed by the owner.
topics.expected: Each role receives only the minimum access needed, with changes left for an authorized administrator.
topics.activity: Complete an offline access matrix for fictional users and sample resources.
topics.mistakes: Shared accounts weaken accountability, and administrator access should not be used merely for convenience.
keyPoints: Users and groups help organize identity.
Permissions should match work responsibilities.
Never bypass approved access processes.
topics.summary: Least privilege connects identity to only the resources and actions required for an authorized task.

topics.title: Ownership and filesystem permissions
objectives: Interpret basic read, write, and execute permissions.
Explain the risks of excessive access.
topics.definition: Filesystem permissions define which actions owners, groups, and other users may perform on an object.
topics.explanation: Permission models commonly distinguish read, write, and execute rights for an owner, a group, and other users. Directory permissions affect listing and traversal differently from file permissions. Effective access can also be influenced by groups, access-control lists, mount options, or application behavior. A safe review uses approved observations and recommends changes only through the system owner's process.
topics.importance: Excessive permissions can expose data or allow unauthorized changes; overly restrictive permissions can disrupt legitimate work.
steps: Identify the object type and owner from approved documentation.
Read the permission categories and their intended users.
Compare access with the documented business need.
Ask the owner to validate any proposed change before implementation.
topics.example: A shared office cabinet allows visitors to view a posted schedule but reserves changes for the coordinator.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional sample report file is readable by its team but not by unrelated roles.

terms.meaning: Allows viewing file contents or listing directory entries, subject to context.
Allows modifying an object or directory entries, subject to context.
Allows running a file or traversing a directory, depending on object type.

topics.diagram:
OWNER | GROUP | OTHER
READ · WRITE · EXECUTE
Interpret with object type and effective identity
topics.demonstration: On paper, translate a fictional permission matrix into allowed read, change, and traversal actions.
exercise: Review three fictional file permission rows.
Compare each row with the documented role that needs access.
Write a recommendation for one excessive permission without changing it.
topics.expected: The learner explains the intended access and routes a possible correction to the owner.
topics.activity: Use an offline permission matrix with fictional files and roles.
topics.mistakes: A permission string alone may not describe effective access; group membership and additional controls matter.
keyPoints: Permissions differ for files and directories.
Effective access depends on identity and configuration.
Changes require owner approval and testing.
topics.summary: Permission review is contextual: compare effective access to documented need and leave changes to authorized owners.

topics.title: Processes and services
objectives: Distinguish a process from a service.
Describe how an approved inventory supports safe review.
topics.definition: A process is a running program instance, while a service is a background capability managed by the operating system or an application platform.
topics.explanation: A service may start at boot, run under a dedicated account, and create one or more processes. Administrators maintain service inventories so they can relate running components to business needs and owners. Process and service state can change over time, so a timestamp and collection context matter. Introductory review should use a prepared inventory or authorized read-only view rather than stopping or changing a service.
topics.importance: Unexpected or unnecessary services may warrant owner review, but disruptive changes can affect availability.
steps: Read the approved service inventory and collection timestamp.
Match each service to a documented owner and purpose.
Flag unknown entries for clarification rather than stopping them.
Record observations without changing service state.
topics.example: A building's heating service is the function; a running boiler is one component supporting it.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional service catalog identifies a training web process and its responsible application team.

terms.meaning: A running instance of a program.
A managed background function provided by software.
The ability of an authorized user to access a system or service when needed.

topics.diagram: SERVICE DEFINITION → MANAGER → ONE OR MORE RUNNING PROCESSES
topics.demonstration: In a paper inventory, connect a named service to its owner, purpose, and sample process label.
exercise: Read the fictional service inventory.
Identify entries with no listed owner.
Draft a question asking the owner to confirm whether an entry is still required.
topics.expected: The learner flags uncertainty for review while preserving the running system state.
topics.activity: Review only the course's fictional process/service table or an explicitly approved local read-only display.
topics.mistakes: Do not terminate an unfamiliar process or disable a service based on its name alone.
keyPoints: A service is a function; processes implement running work.
Ownership and business purpose provide important context.
Stopping services can disrupt availability.
topics.summary: Use a maintained inventory to understand processes and services, and escalate unknowns without making unapproved changes.

topics.title: Logs, timestamps, and evidence
objectives: Describe what logs can contribute to a review.
Identify context needed before drawing conclusions from an entry.
topics.definition: Logs are records of system, application, or security events created to support operations and investigation.
topics.explanation: A useful log entry may include a time, source, event type, and outcome, but fields vary by product. Clock differences, retention gaps, and collection methods affect interpretation. Logs may contain sensitive information and should be handled according to the owner's retention and access policy. Preserve the source and note time zone and provenance when working with approved training data.
topics.importance: Accurate context helps teams correlate events and avoid false conclusions.
steps: Confirm the source and time zone of the sample.
Check the collection method and date range.
Separate direct observations from hypotheses.
Preserve the original and share only approved, minimized excerpts.
topics.example: A doctor's note needs a date, author, and context before a reader can understand what happened.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional event list shows a failed login followed later by a successful login; the sequence alone does not prove who controlled the account.

terms.meaning: A recorded time associated with an event.
Information about where evidence came from and how it was handled.
The period for which records are stored and available.

topics.diagram: SOURCE + TIME ZONE + COLLECTION METHOD + EVENT → CAREFUL INTERPRETATION
topics.demonstration: Compare two fictional records with different time zones and note why their order cannot be assumed until normalized.
exercise: Read a fictional log excerpt in the course workbook.
Record the source, time zone, and fields present.
Write one observation and one question that remains unanswered.
topics.expected: The learner avoids attributing an event to a person without sufficient corroborating evidence.
topics.activity: Annotate a local fictional log sample and preserve its original text.
topics.mistakes: A log entry can be incomplete, delayed, or misconfigured; do not treat a single event as conclusive attribution.
keyPoints: Logs require source and time context.
Evidence should retain provenance and integrity.
Sensitive records must be minimized and protected.
topics.summary: Logs are valuable evidence when handled with context, provenance, privacy, and careful limits on conclusions.

quiz.prompt: What does a shell do?
choices: Interprets commands in a command-line environment
Physically connects a computer to power
Proves a system is authorized for testing
Stores every file in a network
quiz.explanation: A shell interprets commands and provides an interactive environment.
quiz.distractorNote: The terminal is an interface; neither it nor the shell grants authorization.

quiz.prompt: What is an absolute path?
choices: A path that begins at the filesystem root
A path based only on the current folder
quiz.explanation: An absolute path identifies a location from the filesystem root.
quiz.distractorNote: Relative paths depend on the current working directory.

quiz.prompt: What is the safest beginner approach when a command's effect is unclear?
choices: Pause and consult approved documentation or the instructor
Try it on a production server
Add more options until it works
quiz.explanation: Understanding the effect and staying within the local training scope prevents unintended changes.
quiz.distractorNote: Higher privileges or production testing increase risk rather than resolve uncertainty.

quiz.prompt: How should a reviewer handle a configuration value that looks like a secret?
choices: Avoid copying it and follow approved redaction and reporting procedures
Paste it into a public note
Send it to an unrelated account
quiz.explanation: Sensitive values should be minimized, protected, and handled through approved processes.
quiz.distractorNote: Exposure or unapproved changes can create additional risk.

quiz.prompt: What is the principle of least privilege?
choices: Grant only access needed for a defined task
quiz.explanation: Least privilege limits identities to the access their responsibilities require.
quiz.distractorNote: Broad privileges and shared identities weaken accountability and increase impact.

quiz.prompt: Why should permission findings be interpreted with context?
choices: Effective access may depend on identity, object type, groups, and other controls
Permission strings always prove a breach
All directories behave exactly like files
quiz.explanation: Access depends on multiple configuration elements, not a single displayed value.
quiz.distractorNote: A permission display is evidence to interpret, not a complete explanation by itself.

quiz.prompt: What should you do with an unfamiliar service in a review?
choices: Record it and ask its owner to confirm its purpose
quiz.explanation: The owner can confirm business purpose; unapproved state changes may interrupt availability.
quiz.distractorNote: Names alone do not establish whether a service is harmful or unnecessary.

quiz.prompt: What context is important when interpreting a timestamp?
quiz.explanation: Source and time-zone context are needed to correlate records accurately.
quiz.distractorNote: Unrelated interface preferences do not resolve time interpretation.

quiz.prompt: What is log provenance?
choices: Information about where evidence came from and how it was handled
quiz.explanation: Provenance helps establish the source and handling history of evidence.
quiz.distractorNote: Provenance is about evidence context, not interface or credential details.

quiz.prompt: Who should approve a change to a live system configuration?
choices: The responsible system owner through an approved change process
Any learner who can view the file
quiz.explanation: System changes should follow the owner's authorization and change-management process.
quiz.distractorNote: Technical ability to access a file is not permission to change it.

modules.title: Windows Foundations for Security Work
modules.description: Understand Windows accounts, files, permissions, processes, logs, built-in protections, and safe local inspection practices.

learningIntroduction.meaning: Windows is an operating system used on personal computers, business workstations, and many server environments.
learningIntroduction.whyLearn: Security professionals need to understand Windows structure and control concepts to interpret approved system evidence and communicate useful recommendations.
learningIntroduction.jobUse: A penetration tester works within client-approved scope and may review fictional inventories, configuration records, or a local lab; changing a system requires separate owner approval.
learningIntroduction.outcomes: You will recognize key Windows components, explain identity and access controls, and read local training examples without disrupting services or exposing private data.

learningObjectives: Describe the roles of the Windows desktop, filesystem, registry, and PowerShell.
Explain local accounts, groups, User Account Control, and least privilege.
Interpret NTFS access concepts at a high level.
Distinguish a process, service, and event log record.
Describe updates and built-in protections as parts of a layered defense.
modules.moduleSummary: Windows security depends on identity, access, configuration, updates, and operational monitoring working together. Reviewers should use approved, read-only evidence and understand the distinction between an observation and a change. Event logs need source and time context, and built-in protections require maintenance and appropriate policy. A system owner must approve changes and resolve uncertain findings.
keyConcepts: Windows accounts represent identities; groups help assign access by role.
User Account Control helps limit routine use of elevated privileges.
NTFS permissions determine access to files and directories within a broader security context.
Processes and services describe running programs and managed background functions.
Event logs record events that require source, time, and policy context.
Updates and endpoint protections reduce risk when managed and monitored.

glossary.meaning: An identity used to authenticate and access local or domain resources.
A collection of identities used to assign shared permissions.
A Windows feature that helps prevent unauthorized elevated changes.
The standard Windows filesystem that supports access-control permissions and other features.
A set of entries describing which identities may perform actions on an object.
A hierarchical database used by Windows and applications to store configuration.
A running instance of a program.
A background program or capability managed by Windows.
A collection of time-stamped records about system or application events.
Controls that help prevent, detect, and respond to threats on a device.
A software update that can correct defects or security weaknesses.
A command-line shell and scripting environment for system administration and automation.

interviewQuestions.question: Why is a standard user account preferable for routine work?
interviewQuestions.answer: A standard account reduces the amount of privileged activity available to routine applications and helps limit accidental changes. Elevated access should be granted only through an approved process when necessary.

interviewQuestions.question: What does User Account Control contribute?
interviewQuestions.answer: User Account Control helps separate routine activity from elevated actions and can prompt for approval or credentials. It is one layer, not a substitute for least privilege or other safeguards.

interviewQuestions.question: How would you approach an unfamiliar event log entry?
interviewQuestions.answer: I would verify the log source, timestamp, time zone, collection context, and relevant policy. Then I would distinguish what the record directly shows from hypotheses and preserve the original evidence.

interviewQuestions.question: Why are updates and endpoint protection both important?
interviewQuestions.answer: Updates address known software defects and weaknesses, while endpoint protection can help prevent or detect suspicious activity. They serve different purposes and should be maintained according to approved operational policy.

revisionTopics: Review accounts, groups, and the difference between standard and elevated permissions.
Explain how NTFS permissions relate to owner-approved access.
Compare processes, services, and registry configuration.
Practice reading fictional event records with timestamp and source context.
Summarize how updates and endpoint protection contribute to layered defense.

topics.title: Windows environment and system components
objectives: Identify major Windows system components.
Explain why environment details should be confirmed before review.
topics.definition: A Windows environment combines the operating system, desktop interface, filesystem, configuration stores, and management tools.
topics.explanation: The desktop provides a graphical workspace, while the filesystem organizes programs and user data. The registry stores many configuration settings, and management tools expose system information. Windows editions and organizational policies can differ, so a reviewer should confirm the machine and environment from approved documentation. Use a disposable local lab for exercises and do not assume a personal device is in scope.
topics.importance: Knowing the environment helps avoid inaccurate advice and accidental work on the wrong system.
steps: Confirm the designated training environment and its owner.
Identify the Windows edition using course documentation.
Locate the relevant component in the approved system overview.
Record uncertainty and ask before accessing other devices or data.
topics.example: A building floor plan lists offices, utilities, and access points so an inspector knows which area is being discussed.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional workstation profile describes its Windows edition, user role, and approved lab status.

terms.meaning: The graphical workspace through which a user interacts with Windows.
The organized structure used to store and locate files.
A hierarchical store of Windows and application configuration.

topics.diagram: USER → DESKTOP / APPROVED MANAGEMENT VIEW → WINDOWS COMPONENTS
topics.demonstration: Review a printed system profile and identify the operating-system edition, owner, and lab designation.
exercise: Read the fictional workstation profile.
List two components named in it.
Mark which information would require owner confirmation before an assessment.
topics.expected: The learner can describe the sample environment without treating its details as a real target list.
topics.activity: Use a supplied profile card or local disposable VM welcome screen; do not connect to another device.
topics.mistakes: A device name or Windows logo does not prove ownership, version support, or permission to test.
keyPoints: System details vary by edition and policy.
Confirm the approved environment before reviewing it.
Do not infer authorization from a device label.
topics.summary: Start a Windows review by confirming the environment, owner, and permitted evidence sources.

topics.title: Files, directories, and the registry
objectives: Distinguish filesystem data from registry configuration.
Describe safe handling of system and user data.
topics.definition: Windows stores data in files and directories and uses the registry as a structured configuration database.
topics.explanation: Program files, user profiles, and system folders serve different purposes. Registry keys and values describe settings for Windows and applications, but location and meaning depend on the component and policy. Changes to either files or registry settings can affect availability and security. Review an approved copy or read-only view, minimize personal data, and let the owner approve any modification.
topics.importance: Careful context and handling prevent accidental exposure or disruption during technical review.
steps: Confirm the approved source and its owner.
Identify whether the information is a file or a configuration entry.
Read only the values relevant to the stated purpose.
Redact personal or sensitive content and preserve the original.
topics.example: A filing cabinet holds documents while a building control panel stores settings for lights and access.
topics.cyberExample: A fictional registry excerpt contains a placeholder setting and no real credentials or device identifiers.

terms.meaning: A filesystem container used to organize files and other directories.
A set of personal settings and files associated with a user account.
A named container in the hierarchical Windows configuration store.

topics.diagram:
FILES + DIRECTORIES → DATA
REGISTRY KEYS + VALUES → CONFIGURATION
topics.demonstration: Classify each item in a fictional inventory as a document, application file, user setting, or registry configuration entry.
exercise: Review the supplied fictional inventory.
Label which entries contain user data.
Write a redacted note describing one configuration concern without copying private values.
topics.expected: The learner can distinguish stored data from configuration and avoids changing or exposing sample values.
topics.activity: Complete the classification exercise offline using fictional inventory entries only.
topics.mistakes: Do not edit registry values during an assessment simply to see what happens; configuration changes may affect the system.
keyPoints: Files and registry values are different data stores.
Sensitive user data should be minimized.
Only an owner-approved change process may alter a system.
topics.summary: Windows files and registry configuration need careful identification, privacy-aware review, and owner-approved change control.

topics.title: Accounts, groups, and User Account Control
objectives: Explain how identity and groups support access.
Describe why routine work should avoid unnecessary elevation.
